newsitem.title: USA: Mideast summit ends with no breakthrough.
newsitem.headline: Mideast summit ends with no breakthrough.

text.p: An emergency Middle East summit ended on Wednesday with no deal on any dispute, but Israel and the Palestinians agreed to resume talks and President Bill Clinton appealed to the tense region to give peace a chance.

With the leaders of Israel, the Palestinians and Jordan seated silent and grim behind him, Clinton announced that negotiations to resolve issues not settled in Washington would resume on the Israeli-Gaza border on Sunday.
He insisted this represented a fair success for his risky two-day summit which he called to save the peace process from collapse following bloody Israeli-Palestinian violence last week.
But Clinton had to walk a rhetorical tightrope in claiming success for the summit.

"They were not able to resolve their differences here, but to be fair, when we came together, there were no advance guarantees that there would be large-scale, substantive negotiations," Clinton said.

He added: "The message that I want to send out across the Middle East is: I'm convinced that this process and that these parties are in better shape in their relation to one another than they were two days ago, and please, please, give us a chance to make this thing work in the days ahead."
Israelis called the summit a victory but Palestinians said it had failed because of Israeli intransigence.

"The results of the summit are a great success from the point of view of the government of Israel. All the demands ... we presented in the contacts and in the negotiations we've held night and day since coming here were accepted," Israeli Cabinet Secretary Danny Naveh said on Israel radio.
But senior Palestinian negotiator Hasan Asfour told Reuters in Jerusalem:

"What happened in Washington was an American attempt to absorb the anger and reaction of Palestinians and to give the appearance of success. But the summit has failed because of Israeli intransigence."
Reflecting his concern about the rocky diplomatic road ahead, Clinton said: "Give us some time now to let things cool down. Let's don't overreact, now."
Clinton maintained it was a breakthrough merely for Arafat and Netanyahu to talk and cooperate in the search for peace.

He said the main achievement was that the Israelis and Palestinians "are ready to renew and intensify negotiations on implementing the interim (Israeli-Palestinian peace) agreement with Hebron as the first priority."

Hebron is the last major town patrolled by Israeli troops in the Palestinian-run West Bank and a major summit obstacle was Israeli refusal to honour a year-old accord for a partial withdrawal of those troops.
Netanyahu's hardline government wants stronger Palestinian assurances of security against Arab violence.

Israel refused heavy pressure to budge on that issue, and Clinton said the mid-level negotiatiators, who will begin work under U.S. mediation on Sunday, "want to resolve the problem of Israeli redeployment from Hebron and they want to achieve this as soon as possible."
"To assist them ... I am sending Dennis Ross, our special Middle East coordinator, to the region now," he said.
"The very first meeting will take place on Sunday morning in Erez," on the Israeli-Gaza border, he added.

Another dispute concerned Arab demands that Israel close a new entrance it opened last week in a tunnel near shrines sacred to both Moslems and Jews in Jerusalem -- the initial spark for rioting and gunfights that killed 57 Palestinians and 15 Israelis in Gaza and the West Bank last week.
Clinton said no agreement had been reached on that issue.
Overall, he said, "I don't know that the crisis is over... I hope the level of violence has been brought lower and can remain lower while all the people in the Middle East watch these talks unfold."
